subtype: Stage 6: Adults act on both sides [Response]
passage: Pooja, I'm Vasudha, and since you are new to teaching, let me tell you about Manu. Twenty years ago, when I was vice principal, a boy called Manu was pushing a smaller boy, Chotu, around every lunch. First we made sure Chotu was safe: a teacher at lunch, a seat near friends, his parents told the same day. With Manu I was firm. He missed the class trip, and he wrote an apology he had to mean. But I also asked him, "What do you get from this?" He said nothing for a long time. Then: "At home nobody listens to me. Here they do." So we made him the class sports captain, with rules. Slowly he learned respect could be earned another way.

qa.q: What did Vasudha make Manu in the end?
qa.a: Vasudha made Manu the class sports captain, with rules.

qa.q: What did Manu want when he pushed Chotu around?
qa.a: He wanted to be listened to and respected, because at home nobody listened to him.

qa.q: What does Vasudha's story teach Pooja about handling bullying?
qa.a: Protect the target first, give the child who bullied a clear consequence, and also find out what need drives the behaviour so the child can learn better ways.

qa.q: How might Chotu have felt once the adults acted?
qa.a: Chotu likely felt safer and less alone, with a teacher at lunch, friends nearby and parents who knew.

grounding: It shows a school protecting the target, being firm with the boy who bullied, and also finding and meeting the need that drove him.

passage: The principal was away at a board meeting and exams started in two days, but the class teacher did not wait. Then the teacher called Sachin in. "This stops today. You will fix her notebooks, and you'll miss football this week." Sachin scowled. The teacher's voice softened. "But tell me, what's going on with you lately?" Sachin stared at the floor. Then his chin trembled.

subtype: Stage 6: Adults act on both sides [Response]
passage:
When three children reported Kishore for pushing Aman and taking his lunch money, the headmistress, Himani Ma'am, acted that day.

First she sat with Aman and his father. "You did nothing wrong. A teacher will watch the corridor at break, and my door is open."

Then she called Kishore in. She was firm. "This stops today. You'll miss sports for two weeks and you'll write to Aman about what you did."

Kishore stared at the floor, arms folded.

Then her voice softened. "But I also want to understand. What's going on for you, Kishore?"

After a long silence he said, "At home nobody listens to me. Here, when I'm tough, people do."

Himani Ma'am nodded. "Then let's find you a better way to be listened to." She arranged for him to meet the counsellor every week.

qa.q: What consequence did Kishore get?
qa.a: He'll miss sports for two weeks and write to Aman about what he did.

qa.q: What did Kishore reveal about why he bullied?
qa.a: He felt unheard and powerless at home, and being tough at school made people listen to him.

qa.q: Why is Himani Ma'am's approach balanced?
qa.a: She protects Aman first, is firm with Kishore about consequences, and also asks what drives him and arranges counselling.

qa.q: How might Aman feel after meeting Himani Ma'am with his father?
qa.a: He is likely relieved and safer, knowing a teacher will watch the corridor and that he did nothing wrong.

grounding: Himani Ma'am protects Aman, is firm with Kishore, and asks what unmet need drives him, giving the bully both consequence and support.

"Karthik, sit down. Do you know why you're here?"

"Because of Sunny."

"Yes. You've been hiding his bag and calling him names for weeks. That stops today."

"It was just a joke, Irawati Ma'am."

"Sunny doesn't think so. He's been scared to come to school. For the next two weeks, you'll spend recess with me. And you'll apologise to him, properly."

"...Okay."

"But I want to ask you something else. Why do you do it?"

"I don't know."

"Take your time."

"...My brother's always top of the class. Everyone praises him. At school, when I make jokes about Sunny, the boys laugh. They think I'm cool."

"So you want to be noticed."

"I guess."

"That's something we can work on. There are better ways to be noticed. Would you like to help me run the science club?"

"...Maybe."

qa.a: For the next two weeks.

qa.q: What does Karthik seem to feel when he talks about his brother?
qa.a: He seems overlooked and a bit jealous, wanting to be noticed and admired.

qa.q: Why is it wise that Irawati Ma'am offers the science club?
qa.a: It gives Karthik a better way to earn respect and attention, alongside the consequence, so he can learn other ways to be noticed.

qa.q: What has it been like for Sunny, according to Irawati Ma'am?
qa.a: He has been scared to come to school.

grounding: Irawati Ma'am is firm with Karthik about bullying and consequences, then explores his need to be noticed and offers a better way to earn respect.

subtype: Stage 6: Adults act on both sides [Response]
passage:
In Class 6, I was the bully. I called a boy named Bittu "Kaddu" and tripped him in the line.

Then Zainab Ma'am found out. She moved Bittu's seat next to her desk and told his parents she'd keep him safe. And she told me, very clearly, that I would lose PT for a month and that I had to apologise to Bittu in front of the class.

I was angry. But then she asked me to stay after school and said, "Mridul, what's going on with you?"

I ended up telling her my parents fought every night and I felt like I didn't matter. She listened. She got me into the school's art club and talked to my mother.

She was hard on me and kind to me at once.

qa.q: What nickname did Mridul use for Bittu?
qa.a: "Kaddu".

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when Zainab Ma'am gave the consequence?
qa.a: Mridul felt angry at first, but later felt heard when she asked what was going on.

qa.q: What did Zainab Ma'am do for both children?
qa.a: She protected Bittu by moving his seat and telling his parents, gave Mridul a clear consequence, and also listened and got Mridul support through art club and a talk with the mother.

qa.q: How might Bittu have felt after his seat was moved next to Ma'am's desk?
qa.a: He probably felt safer and relieved that an adult was protecting him.

grounding: Mridul recalls how a teacher protected the boy being bullied, gave Mridul firm consequences, and also asked about the unmet need behind the bullying.

subtype: Stage 6: Adults act on both sides [Response]
passage: Counsellor's note, Monday. After last week's report about Kunal pushing Joseph off the swings and taking his snacks, we met both families today. For Joseph: a buddy at break, a teacher on duty near the swings, and a daily check-in with me for two weeks. He smiled a little when he heard he could come to my room any time. For Kunal: he will lose break-time privileges for a week and write an apology in his own words. But I also asked him, alone, "What's been hard lately?" He was silent for a long time. Then: "Nobody at home listens. Here, when I push, everyone looks." I have set up weekly sessions with him and a meeting with his father on Thursday. He needs a consequence and a better way to be seen.

qa.q: What will Kunal lose for a week?
qa.a: He will lose break-time privileges for a week.

qa.q: What does Kunal's answer 'when I push, everyone looks' suggest he feels?
qa.a: He seems lonely and unheard at home, and pushing others makes him feel seen and powerful at school.

qa.q: Why is it wise for the school to act on both sides?
qa.a: Joseph needs protection and daily check-ins to feel safe, while Kunal needs a consequence plus support to find better ways of getting attention.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel hearing about the buddy and the daily check-ins?
qa.a: Joseph probably feels safer and a little relieved, as his small smile at being told he can come any time suggests.

grounding: Shows a school protecting a bullied child, giving the child who bullied a firm consequence, and asking what need drives him.
